name: Accountability for AI Written Submissions
blurb: Who is responsible when AI drafts regulatory content.
title: Accountability for AI Written Submissions
answer: No regulator has a separate route for AI authored content. Sponsors remain fully accountable for submissions, and where AI produces data supporting a regulatory decision, the FDA expects evidence of the model's credibility for that use.

reading.body:
No regulator has a separate route for AI authored content, so the sponsor remains fully accountable for every submission regardless of which tools drafted it.

Accountability in regulated documents is personal and organisational at the same time. Named authors write, reviewers check, and the sponsor signs off and answers to the regulator. A submission is the sponsor's representation to the agency whatever helped prepare it, so AI changes the drafting process without changing who is answerable for the result. The practical form of that is a named author and reviewer for every section, retained drafts and review records, and a record of which tools were used and how.

The one place AI adds a genuinely new obligation is where it produces data or analysis the regulator relies on. There the FDA expects evidence of the model's credibility for that specific use, under the framework it proposed in January 2025 for AI models in drug and biologic submissions. That is a higher bar than disclosure. Listing a tool supports traceability and inspection readiness, but it does not by itself demonstrate that the model was fit for the purpose it was put to.

What this does not cover is the substance of the credibility framework itself, which is named but not detailed here, nor any comparable requirement outside the FDA's remit. The EU AI Act appears only as a related term, with its 2026 Digital Omnibus amendments deferring high-risk deadlines, and nothing in this data says how that regime would treat a regulatory submission. The dates are also worth reading carefully: the framework was proposed in January 2025, and the material was last reviewed in October 2026, so the position described is the proposed one as it stood at review, not a settled rule.

explainer:
In regulated documents accountability is personal and organisational: named authors write, reviewers check, and the sponsor signs off and answers to the regulator. AI does not change that chain. A submission is the sponsor's representation to the agency whatever tools helped prepare it.

Practical accountability means recording who authored and reviewed each section, keeping drafts and review records, knowing which tools were used and how, and being able to explain any statement. Where AI produced data or analysis that the regulator relies on, the sponsor should be ready to show that model's credibility under the FDA framework.

Why the question will not go away

Regulators, journals and ethics committees all take the same position: a company or an author is responsible for what it submits, however the words were produced. A model cannot sign a document, cannot be deposed and cannot be sanctioned. So the accountability question is really about people and process. Who read the AI draft, what did they check, and what record shows they did it?

The practical model most companies use

The approach that holds up best treats AI output the way a medical writing team already treats a first draft from a junior writer. The draft is useful, it saves time, and it is never submitted without review. Three things are added for AI. First, the reviewer is told which parts were machine written so attention goes where it is needed. Second, every factual claim, number and citation is checked against its source rather than trusted because it reads well. Third, the review itself is recorded, with the reviewer named, so the record shows a qualified person stood behind the submission.

What goes wrong

The failures seen so far are rarely about AI inventing science from nothing. They are about plausible text slipping through: a citation that does not exist, a number copied from the wrong table, a safety statement softened in paraphrase, or a template phrase left in that does not apply to this product. Each of these is caught by ordinary verification, which is why the governance answer is a review step that cannot be skipped rather than a ban on the tool.
